[b]The Rysse Dynasty (1915-1943)[/b] 
(Ignore other nation names in later portions, those are place holders and not nations on the map or in this RP, but placeholders to give example)

  The 6th dynasty of Thýven would open with a heavily weakened monarchy, beset at the whims of parliament and the labour unions which had risen rapidly in the 1890s and early 1900s. Thýven was experiencing rapid industrialisation and a population boom which saw the economy fluctuate frequently as industrialisation threatened to outpace it. These were the issues which faced the newly crowned Harkonn Rysse, the son of Thýgaar Hrð who had abdicated due to mental stress brought upon by the throne. 

As a result of his fathers abdication, there was trepidation from parliament to recognise the young Harkonn, who was only 18, and already sought to change the name of the royal house once more, with some suggesting he be put under a temporary regency. However, ultimately after a period of contention parliament, divided between the Labour and Royalist parties would vote in majority to recognise the new king. 

 On September 2, 1915, about two months following the abdication of his father, he was formally crowned by an Adalist Priest in the royal chapel, with the witness of the Prime Minister and the House Steward, with a new house being declared, that being House Rysse. 

  Seeking to bolster the popularity and strength of the monarchy in public affairs, Harkonn would immediately back a major education reform bill which was going through parliament, backed by the Labour party. The bill sought to secularise the public education system to be in line with modern scientific standards. The bill would pass with wide support and be heralded as a victory for the monarchy.

  In order to eradicate the instability which had plagued the royal household he would formally establish the House Council, which would be appointed directly by the monarch from rank and file public servants to serve as advisors. Unfortunately the appointment process would become fraught, as wealthy industrialists like Jorm Erikson, a notable gold tycoon, and Elef Grimm, a notable railroad owner, sought places on the council. Thankfully, parliamentary intervention permitted Harkonn to avoid the scandal of permitting such infighting, with parliament demanding the right to oversee the approval process. By 1916 the council of 8 individuals had fully been staffed, primarily with labour members.

 Turning his eyes to domestic affairs, Harkonn would embark on a trip across the country in the summer of 1916 to see the state of affairs in the  countryside and the city, being greatly concerned by a lack of literacy, transportation, and various other matters which seemed commonsense, but had been taken up by the laissez-faire attitude of his father. 

  In a speech to workers at a factory in the town of  Tézholme Harkonn would announce plans to enact and back a variety of populist and social reforms to ensure the stability of the nation and the security of the economy. These reforms, while not detailed, would soon come to fruition in a rapid succession of bills passed by parliament, most backed by the king.

  In 1916 he would approve a controversial universal suffrage bill, which would permit women to vote. In 1917-18 motions would begin for the formation of a national bank, funded by the labour unions, although this wouldnt formally be founded until 1920. In 1918 he would become the first monarch to visibly open in a public election, wherein the Labour party would win the majority for the first time since the dissolution of the Lyngaard. 

  The arrival of the 1920s in Thýven saw the advent of the public radio (1919) and the rise of car usage across the country as public wealth began to increase thanks to new labor laws relating to time off and efficient work models. The monarchys popularity was also at an all time high due to its more personable nature. In July 1920 Harkonn would make the first radio speech by a member of the government, declaring that a new era of monarchy had arrived, the era of Liberal Monarchy. 

  Liberal Monarchy was received well by the general populace, especially as smooth working relations with parliament persisted, primarily thanks to strong backing by the Labour Party.  

  In October of 1920 Harkonn would announce the widespread secularisation of the monarchy and government as a whole, seeking to detach the powers of the Adaist and Adainist priesthoods from the government. Enacting a widespread purge of religious advisers from all government offices and positions. The purge would prove divisive among the populace of which was 94% religious, affiliated between both schools of religion. With protests beginning in the winter of 1920 against the actions. Hoping to appease the monarch and the peoples the Labour party would issue a compromise permitting the priesthood's non-voting seats within parliament.

In March of 1921 Harkonn would be confronted with a constitutional crisis, as more conservative members of the parliament, members of the Royalist Party, primarily consisting of those nobles who still held power, attempted to recognise his younger sister Jula, the duchess of Trnholme, as the monarch, even going as far as to attempt to coronate her. As a result of the matter, Harkonn would attempt to suspend parliament, but would face fierce opposition from the Labour party as a result. In order to ease tensions, the Labour party would move to gain the support of the Supreme Court against the Royalist Party. The case would be heard between July and August of that year, with the court seeking the backing of the religious courts to Harkonns claim to the throne. Ultimately in September 1921 the court would hand down a ruling in favor of Harkonn and the Labour party, thereby allowing for parliament to pass a censure act to halt and delegitimize the claim that had been fabricated by Jula. 

Following this crisis a radical shift in parliament and the monarchy would begin, primarily as a reaction to the attempts by the traditionalists to undermine the constitutional order of things. With Harkonn declaring in a speech to the country in November of 1921 that the era of Liberal Monarchy had entered into its next phase, full backed reforms based on the ideals of nationalism and secularism.

 The cry of nationalism and secularism would come to dominate the remainder of Harkonn and even his son Jøllyns reign, which would seek to empower parliament and the monarchy to work as one unified branch, creating a hybrid form of labor backed autocratic-parliamentarianism.  Of the early reforms under this second phase of Liberal Monarchy would be the formal enshrinement of popular sovereignty in 1922 with the second constitutional quorum being called to address the question in the summer of 1922. 

 In 1923 the formal state ownership and oversight of any form of media, which had been established following the civil war, as a compromise with the monarchy in the 1864 constitution was formally lifted, thereby opening the constitution further. Unrest in 1923 would see an assassination attempt occur against Harkonn by religious extremists and Deyn Independence Workers, who allegedly sought to free the duchy of Deyn from the crown, which had held sway over the title to the island duchies since the 1770s following the Albic-Thýven war. This would lead to the creation of the One State One Strait policy in 1923, which would seek to bring the administration of the Duchy of Deyn closer to that of the mainland. The policy would be expanded in 1930 to include all Islands in the White Strait, thereby solidifying control of the strait. 

The elections of 1923 would see the Labour Party further solidify their majority in the parliament thereby further solidifying support for the ideals of Liberal Monarchy. Although the Royalists attempted to contest the election results, they failed due to a strong hold upon the state apparatus by the Labour party. 

In 1924 Harkonn would seek to expand the franchise of women within the government, ordering the presence of equal pay amongst both genders, a motion that was pushed back and struck down by the Labour party, which feared that the stances of feminist groups that were advocating for equal pay and labor practices were too radical for the stability of the government. This would lead to Harkonn dragging the bill before the supreme court with the hopes of overturning the Labour party, marking the first time a monarch had attempted to push a bill through parliament via the courts. The court would rule in favor of Harkonn, causing various members of the labour party to resign their seats in parliament. 

1925 would see Harkonn formally recognise his two year old son Jøllyn Rysse as the heir to the Rysse dynasty, with Parliament formally backing Jøllyns claim to the throne. This acted to avoid a potential succession crisis akin to that which led to the contestation of Harkonns reign following his fathers abdication. 

As the country began to formally open up to foreign trade in the early 20s, spurred on by pro-trade laws passed in the 1910s, a new artistic flourishing would arise, inspired by the nationalist movement, a romanticisation of early Thýven history would be pushed by artistic institutions, ending the drive for foreign artistic ideals that had arisen post-1860s as the country sought to stabilise its image on the world stage.

Taking advantage of the sudden drive in nationalist art, Harkonn would pursue a unified national art form, focused on austere and medieval art. Several bills passed between 1925-1926 would see the formation of the National Arts Council, which would set national standards for artistic expression. While heavy proponents for limited government accused Harkonn and the Labour party of leading propaganda, they would receive little attention. 

In 1925 a bill formalising a standard minimum wage would be passed and approved by Harkonn, the following year in 1926 a bill ensuring widespread worker protections would be put in place, including an early 1927 bill which allowed for collective bargaining.

Unfortunately in 1927 a poor national crop in Aïnthaar, one of the leading producers of wheat and grain on Eadora would see wheat prices rise rapidly, spurring food prices across the globe, thereby forcing the government of Thýven to enact widespread rationing in order to curtail food runs. As prices across the globe rose, the demand for gold would decline aggressively thereby threatening the economy and national bank of Thýven.

Faced with a major economic crisis Harkonn would order parliament to suspend itself, thereby halting the elections of that year. Utilising his widespread popularity he justified the suspension of the elections of 1927 as a necessary evil to combat rampant corruption amongst the government. 

In Late 1927 a stock market crash in neighboring Albin would see the globe enter into a widespread economic recession as trade slowed, and unemployment rose aggressively. Thýven would see an initial reduction of trade by 10% in 1927-28, however, with gold prices plummeting the trade deficit would increase, as economic growth slowed to a near grinding halt.

Blaming blatant corporatism and the aggressive monopolisation of the industries of the nation, Harkonn would issue a state of emergency in 1928, thereby allowing widespread constitutional powers to be granted to the monarchy to deal with the affairs of state, economic, and foreign policy. Harkonn would order the railways of Thýven to be fully nationalised. Moving to consolidate government power over the economy. Furthering his attempts to stabilise the economy he would nationalise the merchant marine, placing it under the royal navy. He would order in 1930 the formal nationalisation of the gold industry across the board, seizing and even arresting the heads of the various mining companies which refused to comply.

In 1931 he would formally declare the third phase of Liberal Monarchy by launching a widespread purge of the nobility and parliament, which had remained a puppet of the monarchy since 1927. He would formally declare the Labour-Monarchist party as the sole national party in summer of 1931 and would move to place pro-Harkonn officials within all offices across the country. Protests would erupt in Fall of 1931 as a result of this heavy monarch overreach, leading the Harkonn to increase the provisions of the state of emergency to include the armed forces, placing the armed forces under his direct control. In 1932 he would enact a purge of the House Council which had remained under little change since its creation in 1916. However, the purge was justified under the fact that the majority of the council was aging and not in line with Liberal Monarchy. 

Protests would erupt in May of 1933 as mass layoffs from non-state owned factories violated prior labor union agreements, as a result of this Harkonn and the Labour-Monarchist party would enter discussions with the unions to form a super-union known as the General Confederation of Labor, which would work closely with the government to ensure the consistent protection of workers across all industries was maintained. 

It was around this time that the government and monarchy began to take on a more militaristic look as the finalisation of the union of the armed forces under the crown was completed, with King Harkonn frequently appearing in military uniform in public. It would also be around this time that a third tenet would be added to the ideals of Liberal Monarchism, that being Militarism. Recognising the importance of a strong national military King Harkonn would in 1934 begin a program of rapid military development and armament, much to the concern of Thývens allies who would attempt to raise the issue with the World Union Organisation, however, most of the nations on the High Council, including Aïnthaar, would brush off any threats posed by Thýven. 

By mid-1934 Harkonn had begun to empty the government of useless bureaucrats, and would begin replacing them with military officers, marking a dramatic shift in policy by the state, and disgruntling the older generations who had been sidelined by the radical shift in the government. Protests would break out among the nobles in the summer of 1934 as they attempted to reclaim some form of power for themselves. 

However, this would end in the Stronem declaration, which was passed in October 1934 which would see the nobility formally stripped of their titles and excess lands and political influence, with Harkonn handing over administration of former noble lands and estates to the armed forces. From 1934-1937 it is believed that nearly 400 nobles were arrested under the declaration and either deported or placed in prison. For those nobles lucky enough to curry favour in the armed forces and government, they would remain unaffected by the declaration. 

Unfortunately public opinion of Liberal Monarchy had begun to turn by the end of 1935 as the radical policy shifts still had done very little in effect to fully restore the economy beyond lowering inflation and increasing production very minutely. Protests would break out in January of 1935 as bread prices still remained high, and unemployment still stood at nearly 32%. This would prompt the Labour-Monarchist party at the behest of Harkonn to pass the Social Security Bill, which would see a proper social security system instituted under the powers of the National Bank of Thýven. In April of 1935 Harkonn and the LMP would unveil the first five year plan which would lay out a five-year economic and social development plan aimed at stabilising the country and further ensuring its economic development. 

The plan would aim to streamline import and export regulations and place them under a single office for National Trade, the issuance of Public Debt and Securities, and increasing industrial outreach. 

The plan would formally be adopted in July of 1935 and would see slow progress as the government worked closely with the General Confederation of Labour to ensure the demands of the workers were met. In Late 1935 Harkonn would make his first foreign trip to the neighboring state of Atai, a Sarcine state that had adopted a form of Republican Nationalism, run by the armed forces. It was here that Harkonn met with president Kāmen of Atai, the strongman who had maintained power over that country's government for over a decade by the mid-30s. Kāmens  regime had been widely criticised as antithetical to democratic principles by the World Union Organisation, with them being formally kicked out in 1933, however, their economic recovery following the 1927 crash had been enormous enough to catch the eye of king Harkonn. 

Kāmen and Harkonn would remain good friends until the death of Harkonn in 1945. 

Following the successful trip to Atai, Harkonn would begin to take a more aggressive approach to the running of the state, issuing a decree in 1936 which would grant Thýven full control over the white strait, much to to chagrin of the Albic state, who would formally issue a threat to Harkonn demanding he release control of the strait. 

In response to the letter from the Albic state he would appoint his second cousin Vayn, the third duke of Deyn, and a lieutenant in the armed forces, governor over the strait. This would permit Harkonn to govern the strait without issue, and move military resources to the strait, a move widely condemned by the international community.

On  April 3, 1937, facing international pressure, the Albic states would begin arming itself for war, granting Thýven a thirty day period by which to withdraw their claim from the strait. In response to the threat, Harkonn would order more armed forces onto the Islands of Deyn and Knygta. Issuing a decree ordering the evacuation of the islands over the course of the thirty days. It was clear that Thýven would not back down. 

On April 14, 1937 the state of Atai would formally declare war on the Albic states, moving their armies towards the border of Thýven with the intent to aid Thýen. On April 16th Harkonn would assemble Parliament, formally issuing the Enabling Act of 1937 which would see the constitution of 1864 suspended, declared a state of emergency, suspended the right to public assembly, the right to free press, and granted full martial powers to the armed forces under the crown.

A day later Thýven would declare war on Albin, beginning an immediate blockade of the White Strait. The Thýven Dreadnought Erjk Drynn would open fire on the Albic port city of Vessle, with bombings beginning on the islands off the coast of the Albic states.

 Aided by Atai the blockade against the Albic states was expanded to include all 1,200 miles of the eastern coastline. 

The initial victories of Thýven in mid to late April are often credited with the rapidfire attacks committed by the army of Thýven which sought to overwhelm Albic defense posts across the seaboard. Indeed these blitz attacks would continue into May as Aïnthaar and Thrn would begin to stir to attention. 

The war would wage on with lessening strength through the summer of 1937 as the king was frequently occupied by stressors within the nation itself, spurred on by anti-nationalist factions that had arisen in parliament following the Enabling Act. As a result, and fears that Aïnthaar would mobilise formally (of which it had been planning to do so but had henceforth maintained a strict lendlease), Harkonn would formally call off the war, agreeing to demilitarise the strait, much to the anger of the nationalists in parliament.

On January 2, 1938 the governments of Aïnthaar, Thrn, and representatives from the Albic states would meet with foreign minister Syla Hostjn with the hopes of fully demilitarising the government of the white strait and placing it under protectorate status, however, Syla having been ordered by Harkonn not to grant such a concession, would refuse, stating bluntly that The strait is ours.. This declaration would anger the representatives from Aïnthaar who would threaten harsh grain sanctions against Thýven if they did not yield to the demands of the representatives. 

 On January 12th after several days of refusals and beating around the bush, the government of Thýven, already on edge due to a rise in anti-monarchist sentiment due to economic damages done by the war, as well as fears that the image of Thýven had been damaged and would cause major issues in rebuilding, a deal to demilitarise the strait was reached. 

Following the signing of the White Strait Treaty, which saw the strait demilitarised, and Albic-Aïnthaar patrols established to ensure demilitarisation was maintained, the government of Thýven would see a revolt by the ultra-nationalist monarchist elements which saw the loss of control of the strait as a weakening of the monarchy. 

Fearing for the stability of the monarchy, Harkonn would summon a third constitutional quorum, however, the matter would cause great controversy due to the fact that the quorum consisted solely of members of the Labour-Monarchist party, with all other political members being barred from the quorum.

Protests would break out in the summer of the quorum, with anti-monarchists surrounding the parliament building where the sessions were being held, forcing Harkonn to summon the military to enact a blockade around the structure, and members of the quorum being escorted out by members of the royal guard through a secret tunnel under parliament.

On August 2, 1938 Harkonn would order mass arrests of the protestors citing the suspension of the right to assemble if which was removed in the Enabling Act of 1937. The state would begin a crackdown by August 4th with police conducting mass arrests through that week. On August 12th parliament would pass the Directive For Detention which would permit the armed forces to begin the construction of mass detention centers. 

In November of that year the 3rd Constitutional Quorum would formally announce the 1938 constitution which would fully centralise the state under the military and the crown. Following this Harkonn would declare the fifth phase of Liberal Monarchy, which would see the total establishment of a centralised and unitary state. The last of the nobles would be purged in 1939, and the fullness of the military unleashed upon the government. By 1940 the first formal detention center would be opened in Knygta.

Questions arose over the nature of the detention center by the international community who had raised the issue over the military nature of the centers. As a result Harkonn would formally place the administration of the center under local police, of whom were posited as non-military, although the majority of the administration of the duchy was still under de facto military control. 

The fifth phase of Liberal Monarchy is often considered the most dictatorial and one of the shortest phases lasting from 1940-1944, under this fifth phase the government would formally nationalise the entire economy under the crown and the basic rights of the citizens were removed. It would see the formal enshrinement of the Labour-Monarchist party in politics and would see the rise of the Proxy-Democracy, wherein elections would be held in the localities by military leaders in order to ensure the continued support of the monarchy on the administrative front.

The economy during this period would suffer greatly as the  General Confederation of Labour (GCL) found itself increasingly being entrenched by the government, with political and top level positions being filled by monarch appointed military officials. Unemployment had dipped very little under the first five year plan, only dropping to 30%, prices had continued to rise, wherein the stability of the National Bank was drawn into question. 

As a result of this Harkonn would declare the second 5-year plan in 1941 which would focus on increasing the industrial capacity of the state under the crown controlled industries, wherein exports would be government controlled, a new government office would be formally introduced that would oversee foreign trade known as the Thýven State Office for Trade and Relations (TSOTR), which would control both foreign relations and trade. New factories and public works projects would be initiated, including a formal overhaul of the national highway system which would begin in 1942. 

Unfortunately, Harkonn Rysse would never see the completion of his second plan as he died of a mysterious heart attack a year later in 1943, throwing the government into chaos.
